solutions.check: 31 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Roger somebody or other to discuss this country?

definitions.text: Roger somebody or other to discuss this country?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone needs a word with a person and a topic of conversation about a nation
setter's reading: Private Eye's long-running euphemism for sex is holding talks about a particular East African state

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye coined 'Ugandan discussions' as a coy phrase for a sexual liaison, after a party guest claimed she had been discussing that country upstairs. To roger is British slang for having sex with.
explanation.definitionFit: The East African republic is the nation whose name supplies the magazine's famous euphemism for sexual encounters.

clue.text: Rodent Gordon – ugh! – going ballistic

indicators.note: someone going ballistic flies into a rage and loses all order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Gordon loses his temper and swears in disgust at a rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundhog, or woodchuck, is a North American burrowing marmot, a member of the squirrel family of rodents.

clue.text: Balls-like crackpot

blocks.note: first meaning: resembling nuts, which is slang for testicles
second meaning: mad, eccentric, barmy

explanation.walkthrough: Nuts is slang for testicles, so something like them is, in a jokey sense, full of nuts.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means crazy or eccentric, a crackpot's mental state, and literally means full of or like nuts.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Answer: Ed's commitment is claptrap?

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for answer
a load is a burden or commitment, and the possessive names the Labour shadow chancellor by his surname

explanation.surface: A question about what Ed Balls has promised, with the cynical suggestion that it is all nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was Labour's shadow chancellor; the possessive 'Ed's' turns his surname into the end of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang phrase for nonsense or rubbish, the same as claptrap, meaning empty talk not worth believing.

clue.text: To cry after pisspoor act is a bad thing for luvvies

indicators.note: a pisspoor version of something is badly botched, so the letters that follow come out scrambled
after tells us the crying word is placed behind the scrambled one rather than in front

blocks.note: taken as written
to call out is to cry out

explanation.surface: Actors fear hearing jeers after a dreadful performance.
explanation.walkthrough: Luvvies is British slang for theatrical actors, especially gushing ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A catcall is a shrill jeer or whistle of disapproval from an audience, which no performer wants to hear.

clue.text: (& 15/24dn.)Offensively worthless Andy's penis is out – a chat is out

indicators.note: the two letters spelling is are put out, dropped from the preceding name and member
out means wrong or disordered, so all the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tabloid scandal: some Andy has exposed himself, and now everyone is gossiping.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'is out' removes the closing IS from PENIS; the leftover letters join A CHAT and are rearranged at the second 'out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes goods of low price and poor quality that are also unpleasant or vulgar, worthless in an offensive way.

clue.text: "Turn over" hint on having a stiffy

blocks.note: a tip is a hint or piece of advice
slang: sexually aroused, erect

explanation.surface: A smutty suggestion: someone with an erection is told to roll over.
explanation.walkthrough: A stiffy is British slang for an erection; in a down clue 'on' simply puts one piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: To tip up is to tilt something so it overturns, as a cart or seat does, which is to turn it over.

clue.text: Sun is back in one line agenda – prepare for the worst!

definitions.note: an exclamation of despair rather than a verb phrase

indicators.note: going back means the word for the star is read from right to left
in places the turned word inside the list word

blocks.note: one is the indefinite article a
L is the abbreviation for line
an agenda is a list of items
Sol is the Latin name for the sun

explanation.surface: A newspaper's single-minded campaign returns, and readers are warned to brace themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' looks like the tabloid newspaper, but here it is the Latin name for our star.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry declares total defeat, the state of mind of someone bracing for disaster with nothing left to hope for.

clue.text: Recoil at terrorists stocking drink

indicators.note: stocking means holding in stock, so the words keep the solution among their letters

blocks.note: the end of the first word, the whole second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone flinches at the sight of terrorists, perhaps in a café.
explanation.definitionFit: A latte is a coffee drink made with espresso and plenty of steamed milk.

clue.text: Having revealed your sexual inclination, climax – result!

blocks.note: someone who is out has openly declared their sexuality
to come is slang for reaching orgasm

explanation.surface: Someone celebrates coming out and a sexual high point in one triumphant cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Result!' is British slang for a good outcome, so the exclamation mark is part of the surface cheer.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome is the result or consequence of an action, process or event.

clue.text: Refined sex needs protective support

indicators.note: something protective wraps around what it guards, so the support word encloses the sex word

blocks.note: a pole is a supporting post
it is a coy word for sex or sex appeal

explanation.surface: Sex, a prim voice says, should come with protection.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex is a crossword staple, from phrases like 'doing it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Polite means courteous and well mannered, cultivated in behaviour, as a refined person is.

clue.text: (& 25ac.) "Barely lust!" Joy snapped grabbing penis at its centre

indicators.note: something snapped is broken apart, so these letters fall into a new order
the centre of a five-letter word is its third letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the middle letter of the word

explanation.surface: A woman called Joy loses patience with a partner whose desire is fading.
explanation.walkthrough: Grabbing adds the single kept letter to the scrambled pair of words before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Only just means by the narrowest margin, scarcely or hardly, so the adverb barely fits exactly.

clue.text: One who puts pressure on idiot dealer

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece placed on another comes after it, so the pressing word is sent second

blocks.note: a dope is a fool
someone who pushes, pressing on others

explanation.surface: Someone leans hard on a fool who is dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'A on B' puts A after B, so the pressing word follows the fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A dope pusher sells illegal drugs, and a dealer in slang is exactly someone who sells narcotics.

clue.text: Light a few twists as sign that you've had enough

indicators.note: twisting turns things about, so the letters before it are wrung into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lights a few joints and rolls them up until they cannot take any more.
explanation.definitionFit: Waving a pale banner is the traditional signal of surrender, telling the enemy you give up and want the fighting stopped.

clue.text: Scoring is futile: fail to reach satisfactory climax

blocks.note: a try is a score in rugby
in vain means without success, to no avail

explanation.surface: A frustrated lover finds all effort useless and cannot finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoring' looks sexual in this surface; it is the rugby try. The definition is the setter's smutty gloss on failing.
explanation.definitionFit: To make an effort without success means never achieving the desired result, here pictured as an unsuccessful sexual finish.

clue.text: see 5dn.
(& 18ac.) Slush fund finally takes the piss out of the police?

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: goo is sticky sludge or slush
the final letter of the word
to guy someone is to mock or ridicule them

explanation.surface: A secret slush fund is used to make fools of the police, a corruption story.
explanation.walkthrough: To take the piss is British slang for to mock; to guy means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Law officers are, at least in theory, the heroes on the right side, and the question mark flags this as an example.

clue.text: Mayor does broadcast: his forecasts are dire

definitions.note: a description of the person rather than a noun

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered widely, so these letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mayor goes on air and predicts catastrophe for the city.
explanation.definitionFit: A doomsayer is a prophet of disaster, someone always predicting gloom and calamity.

clue.text: see 16ac.
Miliband abandoned caution in Gove's unreliable hands?

definitions.note: describes the thing rather than naming it

indicators.note: abandoned means wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader
taken as written

explanation.surface: Political sniping: the Labour leader throws caution aside to attack the Tory minister's record.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Gove was the Conservative Secretary of State responsible for schools in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Schooling was the government brief Gove held, so the setter jokes it is the thing placed in his untrustworthy care.

clue.text: Live with your partner cook's 50% drug dependency

indicators.note: fifty per cent is a half, so only the front half of the word is kept

blocks.note: the first half of the word
a habit is an addiction

explanation.surface: A couple living together, one of whom has a cocaine habit and only half-cooks.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohabit is to share a home as an unmarried couple, living together with a lover.

clue.text: Support beneath ministerial arses

blocks.note: surface reading: some kind of underpinning, as if for a cushion or chair
setter's reading: the seat in the Commons where senior government members sit

explanation.walkthrough: In the House of Commons the leading members of government and opposition sit on the seats nearest the central table.
explanation.definitionFit: It is literally the seating that holds up the posteriors of ministers and shadow ministers in Parliament.

clue.text: End of banker – paid off, pdq

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, the only one kept
off means gone bad or wrong, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A banker is bought off in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: pdq stands for 'pretty damn quick'.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation means very fast, and rapid is a plain synonym for quick or swift.

clue.text: see 4dn.
see 5dn.
see 11ac.
Common carve-up?

blocks.note: first meaning: shared, held together, as in a shared account
second meaning: a piece of roast meat that gets sliced at table

explanation.walkthrough: 'Carve-up' suggests a shady shared deal; the question mark flags that it really means meat for carving.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means shared by two or more, and as a noun it is a large cut of meat cooked for slicing.

clue.text: Clasp raw legs, centrally spread

indicators.note: centrally points to letters sitting in the middle of the run of words

blocks.note: the end of the first word, the whole second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: An erotic pose: someone grips bare legs, parted wide.
explanation.definitionFit: To sprawl is to spread out untidily, limbs flung wide, as a body or a town does.

clue.text: Lunatic busy roping in Tony's old sidekick for public financial support?

indicators.note: a lunatic version is crazed, so the next word's letters are jumbled
roping in means drawing someone into a group, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Sid James played alongside Tony Hancock in the radio and TV comedy Hancock's Half Hour

explanation.surface: A frantic Tony Blair recruits an old ally to win government funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tony' suggests Blair, but the sidekick is Sid James, Tony Hancock's comic partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A subsidy is a grant of public money given to support an industry, service or price.

clue.text: Maybe House of Windsor's extremely dreary, repulsive ...

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, so only the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: the two end letters of the word
nasty means disgusting

explanation.surface: A republican sneer that the royal family is dull and revolting, running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The House of Windsor is the British royal family; 'Maybe' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynasty is a line of hereditary rulers from one family, and the Windsors are one such royal house.

clue.text: ... crap Queen Elizabeths and King Edwards?

blocks.note: tat is rubbishy junk
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher, so several Elizabeths are ERs

explanation.surface: The rant continues: the queens and kings are rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward is a well-known British potato variety; kings named Edward are ER too (Edwardus Rex), which deepens the royal disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Taters is informal British slang for potatoes, and King Edwards are a popular potato variety, so they are examples.
